updates.body:
On November 25, 2026, between 21:30 UTC and 00:28 UTC, Git Large File Storage (LFS) operations on github.com were degraded. During this time, an average of 2% of Git LFS requests failed, peaking at 4%. Many more requests initially failed but succeeded when Git LFS clients automatically retried them, which caused slower uploads and downloads for affected users. Other Git operations were not affected. This was due to a large volume of automated, unauthenticated traffic that overwhelmed the Git LFS servers in one of our regions, leaving them unable to respond to requests in time.

We mitigated the incident by moving most Git LFS traffic from the affected region to other regions with more capacity. Error rates returned to normal by 00:28 UTC.

We are working to limit the impact of high-volume unauthenticated traffic on Git LFS, and to add capacity in the affected region, to prevent similar disruptions in the future.
The degradation has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.
We've applied a mitigation to fix the issues in Git LFS. We are seeing improvements in telemetry and are monitoring for full recovery.

On November 16, 2026, between 09:30 and 15:55 UTC, some pull request merges on GitHub timed out. On average, 2.9% of merge attempts timed out, with a peak of 7.1% at 15:17 UTC. Some GitHub Actions workflow runs triggered by pull requests were also delayed. Git operations such as push and fetch stayed available, with higher latency. This was a repeat of a shorter event on November 13, between 13:15 and 17:50 UTC, when 1.7% of merges timed out.

Both events had the same cause: some of the storage servers that hold Git repository data reached their disk read bandwidth limits. A merge must be written to every copy of a repository, so one overloaded server slowed merges for every repository it hosts. Read load on these servers had been growing as part of a planned move of repositories to new infrastructure. A disk configuration setting on those servers also made them read far more data than necessary, which cut their usable bandwidth roughly in half. We mitigated the incident by correcting that setting and moving some load away from the busiest servers.

The corrected setting is now applied permanently across our storage fleet. We are adding storage capacity in the affected region and alerting on per-server disk bandwidth so we catch saturation before it affects customers. Sustained merge timeouts will now page our on-call engineers directly. We are also adding capacity checks before moving repositories or traffic onto new infrastructure.

incidents.title: Impact across multiple GitHub products including Actions, Pages, and Copilot products.

updates.body:
On November 11, 2026, from 20:05 to 21:02 UTC, customers experienced delayed or failed Actions workflow starts, webhook errors and delivery delays, slower GitHub Apps API requests, and reduced availability of Copilot features, including Code Review. GitHub Pages builds were also delayed.

Nearly all GitHub Actions runs triggered between 20:18 and 20:55 UTC were delayed or failed, leaving approximately 3.4 million partially created runs that are being canceled. No GitHub Pages deployments completed during the incident. In the Central US data residency stamp, between 20:06 and 20:50 UTC, about 63% of webhook API requests failed and 27% of deliveries were not recorded; those deliveries reached their destinations but remain unavailable to view or redeliver. Between approximately 20:20 and 21:00 UTC, Copilot code review on github.com completed 87% fewer reviews than normal and some other Copilot features were also unavailable.

The disruption was caused by an Azure Cosmos DB regional outage affecting database accounts used by these services. Per Cosmos’s RCA, a configuration change to the Central US gateways exposed a latent race condition under a specific high-load traffic pattern, causing gateway crashes and health-probe failures. Cosmos mitigated by rolling back the change. Service health recovered around 21:02 UTC, and the queued Actions backlog finished processing by 21:21 UTC.

Our follow-up work focuses on validating regional database failover across affected services and developing tested recovery procedures. We are also improving recovery tools to quickly clear stuck Actions checks and runs after incidents so they do not remain uncancelable or block pull request merges.

incidents.title: Incident with Actions and Checks API

updates.body:
On November 9, 2026, between 18:07 and 18:59 UTC, GitHub Actions experienced degraded performance. During this time, some customers saw workflow runs fail to start, update or report status correctly. An average of 28% of workflow runs were affected, peaking at 65% during the worst period of the incident. Once Actions services recovered, some jobs were left in a state that limited available concurrency until the runs were released.

The incident occurred during a planned migration of a core Actions database from GitHub’s datacenter to a new cloud region. After the migration completed, we shifted Actions service traffic to the new region. The volume of requests exceeded the capacity and rate limits configured there, so a portion of requests were rejected and workflow updates failed. Dependent services, including Webhooks, Pages and Copilot code review, saw secondary impact.

We mitigated impact by shifting some of the traffic back to the original region, allowing service traffic to remain within the configured limits. We then increased capacity and rate limits in the new region before gradually shifting traffic back. While this was a one-time migration event for this cluster that is now complete, we are improving how we validate capacity and limits before shifting traffic during remaining migrations, including shifting traffic in smaller steps. To address the stuck runs left after the incident, we are improving our ability to detect and mitigate these runs for future cases as well as readying an API to enable customers to address this themselves.

incidents.title: Incident with Pull Requests, Git Operations and Issues

updates.body:
n November 4, 2026, between 09:35 UTC and 11:43 UTC, customers experienced intermittent errors and timeouts across GitHub.com, primarily on actions that write data. At peak, about 20% of pull request write operations (such as merging, commenting, and reviewing) failed, along with about 10% of issue creates and edits and 10–15% of project item edits. Git pushes over SSH, REST and GraphQL API requests, code scanning uploads, releases, and package operations were also affected, and about 1% of Actions runs were delayed by more than five minutes or failed to start. Overall, nearly 4% of all requests to GitHub.com failed at the worst point. Reads were largely unaffected, and retrying a failed action a short time later usually succeeded.

The incident was triggered by a burst of concurrent updates to the same database record, which tied up all available connections to one of our primary databases. Although that contention cleared, the backlog of waiting requests kept our database connection layer overloaded, and it did not recover on its own. We mitigated the incident by failing over to a new primary database host. Most services recovered by 11:31 UTC, and Actions recovered by 11:43 UTC.

Since the incident, we have disabled the code path that triggered the contention, increased the processing capacity of our database connection layer by 50%, and added alerting to detect this type of overload earlier. We are also improving our procedures so we can fail over sooner in similar situations.

On November 3, 2026, between 15:00 UTC and 22:37 UTC, Git operations over HTTPS on GitHub.com were degraded. Clones, fetches, and pushes over HTTPS were slow, and some failed. For about half of Git HTTPS traffic, median response time rose from under 100 milliseconds to as high as 5 seconds. On average, the error rate was 0.65% and peaked at 1.29% of requests to the service. Git operations over SSH were not affected.

This was due to a buildup of excess connections on the hosts that serve Git HTTPS traffic, which saturated their network capacity and caused slow and failed responses for all clients served by those hosts.

The block also prevented some users of one third-party integration from performing Git operations over HTTPS until we removed it on November 4 at 13:26 UTC.

We are working to alert on sustained Git HTTPS latency sooner and make load balancer mitigations take effect on existing connections immediately.

The impact was triggered by maintenance on a cloud network gateway connecting an Actions service in the GitHub data center to Redis clusters in the Central US Azure region. Impact

We have since fully enforced it and capped the service's concurrent connection attempts. We are extending these limits to other Actions services, adding backoff to retries, limiting how much shared network capacity a single service can use, and improving alerting so we can find the source of connection surges faster.

incidents.title: Incident with Git Operations, Pull Requests and Actions

updates.body:
On October 7, 2026, GitHub had two outages of write operations with the same cause, totaling about 19 minutes. The first ran from 15:06 to 15:16 UTC (about 10 minutes) and the second from 16:52 to 17:01 UTC (about 9 minutes). In both windows, actions that save or change data failed across Git operations, pull requests, issues, GitHub Actions, the API, webhooks, sign-in and authentication, GitHub Apps and OAuth, code scanning, Codespaces, and Copilot. Reading data was largely unaffected.

In the first outage, 5.6% of all web and API requests failed, peaking at 8.9%, and more than 12,000 organizations saw failed requests. Up to 26% of Git authentication requests failed, and 17% of Actions workflow runs failed with infrastructure errors. In the second outage, 6.2% of web and API requests failed, peaking at 9.3%, and more than 11,000 organizations were affected. Up to 25% of Git authentication requests failed, and 19% of Actions workflow runs failed. No databases experienced data loss, and operations retried after recovery succeeded.

GitHub relies on an internal service that keeps track of which database servers should receive new and updated data. While replacing machines that run this service as part of regular maintenance, one of the new machines started with an outdated copy of its records, which still listed database servers we had already retired. When this node came online, it incorrectly modified routing configuration with the outdated records, routing write requests to non-existent database servers.

Each outage ended when one of our established machines with correct configuration became the leader of the quorum and sent the correct configuration. After the first outage, we identified the new machine as the source and paused automated maintenance to stop it from being leader again. At 16:52 UTC, an automated maintenance task that did not honor the pause put it back in charge, and the outage happened again. We shut that machine down at 17:02 UTC and have since removed it, and the automation now honors the pause, which was a new regression due to an update of our puppet infrastructure.

To prevent recurrence, we are clearing retired database servers from the service's records before any new machine is added, and we are keeping new machines from being elected leader until their records have been checked. We are also changing our systems to reject configuration that point to servers that don't exist and to keep using the last known-good settings instead. Finally, we are giving responders a faster way to take a misbehaving machine out of service, and adding alerts so changes like this are spotted within seconds.

We will share a more detailed write-up of these incidents in our monthly availability report, along with the status of the repairs we are making to prevent issues like these in the future.

On November 16, 2026, between 09:30 and 15:55 UTC, some pull request merges on GitHub timed out. On average, 2.9% of merge attempts timed out, with a peak of 7.1% at 15:17 UTC. Some GitHub Actions workflow runs triggered by pull requests were also delayed. Git operations such as push and fetch stayed available, with higher latency. This was a repeat of a shorter event on November 13, between 13:15 and 17:50 UTC, when 1.7% of merges timed out.

Both events had the same cause: some of the storage servers that hold Git repository data reached their disk read bandwidth limits. A merge must be written to every copy of a repository, so one overloaded server slowed merges for every repository it hosts. Read load on these servers had been growing as part of a planned move of repositories to new infrastructure. A disk configuration setting on those servers also made them read far more data than necessary, which cut their usable bandwidth roughly in half. We mitigated the incident by correcting that setting and moving some load away from the busiest servers.

The corrected setting is now applied permanently across our storage fleet. We are adding storage capacity in the affected region and alerting on per-server disk bandwidth so we catch saturation before it affects customers. Sustained merge timeouts will now page our on-call engineers directly. We are also adding capacity checks before moving repositories or traffic onto new infrastructure.

incidents.title: Impact across multiple GitHub products including Actions, Pages, and Copilot products.

updates.body:
On November 11, 2026, from 20:05 to 21:02 UTC, customers experienced delayed or failed Actions workflow starts, webhook errors and delivery delays, slower GitHub Apps API requests, and reduced availability of Copilot features, including Code Review. GitHub Pages builds were also delayed.

Nearly all GitHub Actions runs triggered between 20:18 and 20:55 UTC were delayed or failed, leaving approximately 3.4 million partially created runs that are being canceled. No GitHub Pages deployments completed during the incident. In the Central US data residency stamp, between 20:06 and 20:50 UTC, about 63% of webhook API requests failed and 27% of deliveries were not recorded; those deliveries reached their destinations but remain unavailable to view or redeliver. Between approximately 20:20 and 21:00 UTC, Copilot code review on github.com completed 87% fewer reviews than normal and some other Copilot features were also unavailable.

The disruption was caused by an Azure Cosmos DB regional outage affecting database accounts used by these services. Per Cosmos’s RCA, a configuration change to the Central US gateways exposed a latent race condition under a specific high-load traffic pattern, causing gateway crashes and health-probe failures. Cosmos mitigated by rolling back the change. Service health recovered around 21:02 UTC, and the queued Actions backlog finished processing by 21:21 UTC.

Our follow-up work focuses on validating regional database failover across affected services and developing tested recovery procedures. We are also improving recovery tools to quickly clear stuck Actions checks and runs after incidents so they do not remain uncancelable or block pull request merges.

updates.body:
On November 10, 2026, from approximately 15:00 UTC to 17:55 UTC, GitHub experienced degraded performance affecting repository pages, pull requests, and GitHub Actions. Customers may have seen slow or failed page loads and delays processing pull request updates and merges. Some pull requests continued to display an earlier source-branch commit after the broader service degradation ended. GitHub Actions workflows were delayed for approximately 1.8% of events, peaking at about 7% between 16:30 and 16:50 UTC. Delays were typically 1.5 to 3.5 minutes, up to 10 minutes. The degradation resulted from overload in the shared infrastructure that supports Git operations. Recent changes increased background processing and the work required to compute pull request merges, adding pressure to the same systems used by customer-facing requests. We mitigated the incident by disabling a recent merge-processing optimization, pausing background analysis, and temporarily limiting lower-priority traffic. The temporary limits also restricted access to commit pages for users who were not signed in. Background processing continued to catch up after service health recovered.

We have reduced repeated repository-analysis work and are adding workload-level concurrency controls to better protect customer-facing requests. We are also improving our procedures for safely reducing background load and making pull request synchronization more resilient to temporary failures.

incidents.title: Incident with Actions and Checks API

updates.body:
On November 9, 2026, between 18:07 and 18:59 UTC, GitHub Actions experienced degraded performance. During this time, some customers saw workflow runs fail to start, update or report status correctly. An average of 28% of workflow runs were affected, peaking at 65% during the worst period of the incident. Once Actions services recovered, some jobs were left in a state that limited available concurrency until the runs were released.

The incident occurred during a planned migration of a core Actions database from GitHub’s datacenter to a new cloud region. After the migration completed, we shifted Actions service traffic to the new region. The volume of requests exceeded the capacity and rate limits configured there, so a portion of requests were rejected and workflow updates failed. Dependent services, including Webhooks, Pages and Copilot code review, saw secondary impact.

We mitigated impact by shifting some of the traffic back to the original region, allowing service traffic to remain within the configured limits. We then increased capacity and rate limits in the new region before gradually shifting traffic back. While this was a one-time migration event for this cluster that is now complete, we are improving how we validate capacity and limits before shifting traffic during remaining migrations, including shifting traffic in smaller steps. To address the stuck runs left after the incident, we are improving our ability to detect and mitigate these runs for future cases as well as readying an API to enable customers to address this themselves.

incidents.title: Incident with Pull Requests, Git Operations and Issues

updates.body:
n November 4, 2026, between 09:35 UTC and 11:43 UTC, customers experienced intermittent errors and timeouts across GitHub.com, primarily on actions that write data. At peak, about 20% of pull request write operations (such as merging, commenting, and reviewing) failed, along with about 10% of issue creates and edits and 10–15% of project item edits. Git pushes over SSH, REST and GraphQL API requests, code scanning uploads, releases, and package operations were also affected, and about 1% of Actions runs were delayed by more than five minutes or failed to start. Overall, nearly 4% of all requests to GitHub.com failed at the worst point. Reads were largely unaffected, and retrying a failed action a short time later usually succeeded.

The incident was triggered by a burst of concurrent updates to the same database record, which tied up all available connections to one of our primary databases. Although that contention cleared, the backlog of waiting requests kept our database connection layer overloaded, and it did not recover on its own. We mitigated the incident by failing over to a new primary database host. Most services recovered by 11:31 UTC, and Actions recovered by 11:43 UTC.

Since the incident, we have disabled the code path that triggered the contention, increased the processing capacity of our database connection layer by 50%, and added alerting to detect this type of overload earlier. We are also improving our procedures so we can fail over sooner in similar situations.

On November 3, 2026, between 15:00 UTC and 22:37 UTC, Git operations over HTTPS on GitHub.com were degraded. Clones, fetches, and pushes over HTTPS were slow, and some failed. For about half of Git HTTPS traffic, median response time rose from under 100 milliseconds to as high as 5 seconds. On average, the error rate was 0.65% and peaked at 1.29% of requests to the service. Git operations over SSH were not affected.

This was due to a buildup of excess connections on the hosts that serve Git HTTPS traffic, which saturated their network capacity and caused slow and failed responses for all clients served by those hosts.

The block also prevented some users of one third-party integration from performing Git operations over HTTPS until we removed it on November 4 at 13:26 UTC.

We are working to alert on sustained Git HTTPS latency sooner and make load balancer mitigations take effect on existing connections immediately.

The impact was triggered by maintenance on a cloud network gateway connecting an Actions service in the GitHub data center to Redis clusters in the Central US Azure region. The service's Redis client retried aggressively and redialed those connections. That produced a connection storm that saturated the gateway, with about 90% of connection attempts failing. incidents.title: Degraded availability for GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages and Webhooks

updates.body:
On October 19, 2026, between 15:24 and 16:52 UTC, GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages, and webhooks generated by Actions were degraded. Live updates on GitHub.com and code search were also degraded for part of this time. No data was lost.

Impact

- Workflow status updates, logs, and checks were delayed.
- 5.13% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners were delayed in starting, and 0.02% of workflow runs failed.
- During the first 30 minutes, 8.47% of requests to the Actions jobs REST API returned errors.

Pages deployments and webhooks generated by Actions runs were delayed.

An internal Actions service that stores logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region and immediately retried them from every server at once. The resulting surge of new connections overloaded a shared network link between our data center and that region, which also disrupted other services that use the same link. We mitigated the incident by moving the Actions service off the affected cache servers and reducing connections from other services on the link. We then processed the delayed Actions work. We are continuing to investigate the cause of the initial connection timeouts.

We were already in the process of rolling out a limit on how quickly this service can open new connections, but it was still in shadow mode (logging only, not enforcing) at the time of the incident. We have since fully enforced it and capped the service's concurrent connection attempts. We are extending these limits to other Actions services, adding backoff to retries, limiting how much shared network capacity a single service can use, and improving alerting so we can find the source of connection surges faster.
Actions, Pages and Webhooks are operating normally.

We’re seeing recovery following mitigation and are continuing to monitor.

incidents.title: Incident with Git Operations, Pull Requests and Actions

updates.body:
On October 7, 2026, GitHub had two outages of write operations with the same cause, totaling about 19 minutes. The first ran from 15:06 to 15:16 UTC (about 10 minutes) and the second from 16:52 to 17:01 UTC (about 9 minutes). In both windows, actions that save or change data failed across Git operations, pull requests, issues, GitHub Actions, the API, webhooks, sign-in and authentication, GitHub Apps and OAuth, code scanning, Codespaces, and Copilot. Reading data was largely unaffected.

In the first outage, 5.6% of all web and API requests failed, peaking at 8.9%, and more than 12,000 organizations saw failed requests. Up to 26% of Git authentication requests failed, and 17% of Actions workflow runs failed with infrastructure errors. In the second outage, 6.2% of web and API requests failed, peaking at 9.3%, and more than 11,000 organizations were affected. Up to 25% of Git authentication requests failed, and 19% of Actions workflow runs failed. No databases experienced data loss, and operations retried after recovery succeeded.

GitHub relies on an internal service that keeps track of which database servers should receive new and updated data. While replacing machines that run this service as part of regular maintenance, one of the new machines started with an outdated copy of its records, which still listed database servers we had already retired. When this node came online, it incorrectly modified routing configuration with the outdated records, routing write requests to non-existent database servers.

Each outage ended when one of our established machines with correct configuration became the leader of the quorum and sent the correct configuration. After the first outage, we identified the new machine as the source and paused automated maintenance to stop it from being leader again. At 16:52 UTC, an automated maintenance task that did not honor the pause put it back in charge, and the outage happened again. We shut that machine down at 17:02 UTC and have since removed it, and the automation now honors the pause, which was a new regression due to an update of our puppet infrastructure.

To prevent recurrence, we are clearing retired database servers from the service's records before any new machine is added, and we are keeping new machines from being elected leader until their records have been checked. We are also changing our systems to reject configuration that point to servers that don't exist and to keep using the last known-good settings instead. Finally, we are giving responders a faster way to take a misbehaving machine out of service, and adding alerts so changes like this are spotted within seconds.

We will share a more detailed write-up of these incidents in our monthly availability report, along with the status of the repairs we are making to prevent issues like these in the future.

updates.body: We are investigating a service degradation causing elevated error rates affecting chat and agent requests across all models. Some users may experience failed or slow responses.
We have implemented a fix and are seeing recovery across chat and agent requests. We are closely monitoring the service to ensure full stability.
This incident has been resolved. Error rates affecting chat and agent requests have returned to normal operation.

Aiming to resolve within the hour.

我们确认 CN-NORTH-1 区域的多项 AWS 服务出现严重错误率问题。在此期间，客户调用 AWS API 时会遇到延迟增加和 5XX 错误。客户在使用 AWS 服务管理控制台时也可能遇到错误，部分 AWS 终端节点也可能出现连接问题。工程师已被自动调动并立即开始调查。对于部分服务（例如 EC2），影响主要集中在 cnn1-az1。对于 EC2，我们建议客户尝试在其他可用区中启动实例。我们正在积极核实对根本原因的判断，同时努力减轻对 AWS 服务的影响。我们将在北京时间11月19日早上 2:00 提供下一次更新；如有更多信息，我们会提前发布。| We can confirm significant error rates for multiple AWS Services in the CN-NORTH-1 Region. During this time, customers will experience increased latencies and 5XX errors when calling AWS APIs. Customers may also experiencing errors when interacting with AWS Service Management Consoles, and connectivity issues to some AWS endpoints. Engineers were automatically engaged and immediately began investigating. For some services, such as EC2, impact is primarily limited to cnn1-az1. For EC2, we recommend customers attempt to launch in other Availability Zones. We are actively working on both verifying our understanding of the root cause, and mitigating impact to AWS Services. We will provide another update at 10:00 AM, or sooner if we have additional information to share.

我们已查明导致 CN-NORTH-1 区域多项 AWS 服务出现严重错误率问题的根本原因。我们已观察到初步的恢复迹象，并将继续监控，努力实现全面恢复。工程师已被自动调动，正在继续努力全面缓解所有问题。现有资源（例如 EC2 实例和 RDS 数据库实例）未受此问题影响。此次影响是由一个负载均衡器的问题引起的，该负载均衡器负责将流量路由到 SQS 和 SNS，并为 AWS 内部服务提供 DNS 支持。此问题也影响到了其他 AWS 服务，受影响的服务列表见下文。我们建议客户尽可能重试失败的 API 请求。我们将在北京时间11月19日早上 2:15 提供下一次更新；如有更多信息，我们会提前发布。| We have identified the root cause resulting in significant error rates for multiple AWS Services in the CN-NORTH-1 Region. We are seeing early signs of recovery and continue to monitor and work toward full recovery. Engineers were automatically engaged, and continue to work on fully mitigating all issues. Existing resources, such as EC2 Instances and RDS DB Instances are unaffected by this issue. This impact is the result of an issue with a load balancer that is responsible for routing traffic to SQS, SNS, and for DNS supporting internal AWS services. This impact is also affecting other AWS Services. A list of impacted services is available below. We recommend customers retry failed API requests wherever possible. We will provide another update at 10:15 AM, or sooner if we have additional information to share.

北京时间 2026 年 11 月 19 日 00:15 至 01:36 期间，CN-NORTH-1 区域的多项 AWS 服务出现了严重的错误率问题和 DNS 解析超时。工程师已立即被自动调动，开始查明根本原因并减轻影响。在此期间，客户向 AWS 服务终端节点发出 API 请求时，延迟和错误率均有所增加。现有资源（例如 EC2 实例）未受此问题影响。北京时间 01:03，我们查明根本原因是一个负载均衡器出现问题，该负载均衡器负责将流量路由到 SQS 和 SNS，并为 AWS 内部服务提供 DNS 支持。北京时间 01:15，我们开始观察到初步的恢复迹象，并持续进行缓解工作。北京时间 01:36，影响已完全消除。我们建议客户重试失败的请求。我们预计此问题不会再次发生。该问题已解决，AWS 服务现已恢复正常运行。| Between 8:15 AM and 9:36 AM PST, we experienced significant error rates and DNS resolution timeouts for multiple AWS Services in the CN-NORTH-1 Region. Engineers were immediately and automatically engaged, and began working on both identifying the root cause and mitigating impact. During this time customers experienced increased latencies and error rates for API requests to AWS Service endpoints. Existing resources, such as EC2 instances were unaffected by this issue. At 9:03 AM, we identified the root cause as an issue with a load balancer responsible for routing traffic to SQS, SNS, and DNS that supports internal AWS services. By 9:15 AM, we began observing early signs of recovery, and continued mitigation efforts until impact was fully resolved at 9:36 AM. We recommend customers retry failed requests. We do not expect this issue to reoccur. The issue has been resolved and AWS Services are operating normally.

At 9:03 AM, we identified the root cause as an issue with a load balancer responsible for routing traffic to SQS, SNS, and DNS that supports internal AWS services. By 9:15 AM, we began observing early signs of recovery, and continued mitigation efforts until impact was fully resolved at 9:36 AM. We recommend customers retry failed requests.
